about: Seeded-defect saga corpus (issue #2736, first slice). One row per defect: a small saga with a known saga defect, the defect written down before any version of the saga, and the catch point the corpus expects. The revl verdict is measured by `python3 bench/saga_defects/run.py`; the Temporal port and independently written sagas are the second slice and are not scored here.

systems.temporal: not scored in this slice; the hand port and its score are the second slice of issue #2736

failureModel: One failure is injected after a top-level step of the saga component completes, in program order (the `revl test --sweep` model; docs/fault-tests.md section 9). The sequential, single-fault model does not cover concurrency, clock or random coeffects.

verdicts.compile: the checker refused the saga; the defect cannot reach a run
verdicts.fault-test: the saga compiled and `revl test --sweep` failed at a seeded fault
verdicts.missed: the saga compiled and every sweep unit passed

groups.project: written by the people who built the checker
groups.outside: a saga whose shape was not written by the checker's authors (none in this slice)

defects.description: The inventory hold carries no undo, so a failed checkout would leave the reservation standing. Same defect kind as `missing-undo-auth` (an `effect` with no `undo`), seeded at the other call site of the same saga: the two rows are one defect kind at two call sites, not two defects.

The payment authorization carries no undo, so a failed checkout would keep the charge. Same defect kind as `missing-undo-hold` (an `effect` with no `undo`), seeded at the other call site of the same saga: the two rows are one defect kind at two call sites, not two defects.
The irreversible settlement is written as `effect ... undo`; an emission must be marked `emit` with a `compensate` slot.
A reversible operation is marked `emit`, claiming an irreversibility it does not have.
A host acquisition is undone on a sibling handle, so its own resource would stay open while the teardown reports a clean release.
The author writes the teardown order by hand in a provide-method undo; the inverse reaches an emission, which a bracket inverse may not cross.

The call site gives an irreversible settlement an `undo` instead of a `compensate`; the parser refuses the `undo` keyword there, so this is a parse refusal, not a G6 reversibility check. The `G6` in `expectedCode` is only the hint tag the parser attaches to its generic statement error, so `expectedLine` pins the seeded line as well. Its message is the parser's generic `expected a statement` error, which any typo would also earn, so it is counted as a parse refusal apart from the checker refusals.
Two saga components require each other's provision, so neither can ever activate (G3 is link-time acyclicity of component dependencies, not step order).
The charge's inverse is present and well-shaped but calls a host helper that raises during the unwind.
The settlement's compensation is present but calls a host helper that raises during phase two.
The irreversible settlement declares no compensation, so a later failure has no recorded follow-up action.
The charge for one order is undone by a refund for a different order. The payment store is an opaque host boundary in this saga, so the fault sweep cannot see which order was refunded.

The two inventory holds release each other's sku: the first hold's undo releases the second hold's key and the second's releases the first's. The derived order is mechanically LIFO, but the hand-written inverse targets are swapped, so the first hold's own key survives its step. The provider is Map-backed, so the sweep's host-residue check sees the un-reversed write.

The charge is undone by a refund of half the amount: the inverse is present and well-shaped but reverts only part of the effect. The ledger provider keeps the charged amount in a `Map` and a refund subtracts from it, so half a refund leaves the other half behind; the sweep's host-residue check sees that residue (with a full refund the same saga passes every sweep unit).
defects.changedAfterMeasurement: The first version's provider removed the whole row on any refund, so the defect could not show and the row was measured as `missed`. After that measurement the provider was changed to keep the amount, and the description and the expected verdict (now `fault-test`) were rewritten.

defects.description: The compensation calls a helper that returns success without reversing anything.
The compensation and the hold's own inverse release the same hold; the second release is a silent no-op in this provider.
